surface_mechanism_description: The ALD cycle including sequential pulses of both metal precursors followed by one H2O pulse can be used for doping the ZrO2 films. The chemisorption mechanism of Dy precursor on the surface pretreated by Zr precursor would likely be different from that in the case of Zr precursor adsorbing on the surface pretreated by the Dy precursor.
evidence: It has been demonstrated earlier that some oxides can be deposited from thd-type precursors and H2O in a very similar way. Provided that decomposition of the precursor and precursor ligands does not contribute to the film growth, a possible mechanism of ALD from M(thd)3 (where M is a metal) and H2O could be described using the following chemical reactions nOH + 2M(thd)3(g) = OnM2(thd)6/C0 n + nHthd(g); OnM2(thd)6/C0 n + 3H2O(g) = O3M2(OH)n + (6/C0 n)Hthd(g); where 0/C20 n/C20 6. However, we could not find information on ALD of thin films from Dy(thd)3 and H2O. The behavior of the QCM signal recorded during an ALD cycle also depended somewhat on the sequence of the metal precursors, i.e., whether the Dy(thd)3 was pulsed on the surface previously exposed to ZrCl4 or vice versa. We could see that significant precursor adsorption started 0.5 – 1 s after switching on the first metal precursor (ZrCl4 or Dy(thd)3) pulse (Figure 2). Within the following few seconds the film mass abruptly increased and then began to stabilize. Switching off the first metal precursor pulse caused, however, an additional increase of the mass sensor signal indicating that temperature fluctuations probably contributed to the oscillation frequency of the quartz crystal in both processes. During the second metal precursor pulse, by contrast, we could see marked difference between these two processes. When the Dy(thd)3 pulse was applied after the ZrCl4 pulse, then QCM did not detect considerable mass change (Figure 2a). As the films deposited in the ZrCl4-Dy(thd)3-H2O process contained Dy, we could conclude that Dy(thd)3) was adsorbed but the release of chlorine in reactions with surface species formed during the ZrCl4 pulse compensated the mass increase related to adsorption of surface species that contained Dy. During the H2O pulse and immediately after that, the mass sensor signal decreased significantly, demonstrating that exchange reactions took place and the total mass of the metal precursor ligands replaced in this reaction step was greater than the mass of oxygen and/or hydroxyl groups, which could replace the metal precursor ligands. In the Dy(thd)3-ZrCl4-H2O process, when the ZrCl4 was applied after the Dy(thd)3 pulse, the ZrCl4 pulse caused a significant mass decrease (Figure 2b). By contrast, only minor changes in the mass sensor signal were observed during the H2O pulse. Consequently, the release of metal precursor ligands during the pulse of the second metal precursor was more efficient in the Dy(thd)3-ZrCl4-H2O process than in the ZrCl4-Dy(thd)3-H2O one. This result was in correlation with the data of post-growth studies, which showed that also the thickness growth per cycle was higher in the Dy(thd)3-ZrCl4-H2O process (Table 1). Unfortunately, it was not possible to deduce the mechanisms of surface reactions from the QCM data because the reactions were evidently complex and we could not exclude the effect of temperature fluctuations on the shape of the QCM signal in the experiments. It is worth noting, however, that the temperature fluctuations had markedly weaker effect on the mass increase per cycle (Figure 2) because this parameter was determined from measurements carried out at the same temperature regime, i.e., at the end of the last purge in each ALD cycle.
